name: Implementation Roadmap
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: From Green Light to Go Live: Sequencing the Rollout
lesson.summary: A green light from the decision flowchart is not permission to build the full system at once. This chapter lays out a four-stage implementation roadmap, from scoped discovery through a bounded pilot to full rollout, with evidence-based go and no-go gates at every stage.
lesson.body:
A yes out of the decision flowchart is not a green light to build the full production system. It's permission to start spending real money carefully, and the biggest mistake organizations make at this stage is treating the flowchart's conclusion as if it were already proof the specific design will work in practice. It proves the problem is real and blockchain is a reasonable class of solution. It does not prove your chosen consortium will agree on governance, that your vendor's platform will hold up under real load, or that the people who are supposed to write data every day will actually do it correctly. An implementation roadmap exists to answer those remaining questions in stages, cheaply, with an explicit off-ramp at every stage, before the expensive stage arrives.

The roadmap has four stages, each gated by criteria defined before the stage starts, not decided afterward by whoever is most invested in continuing.

Stage one is scoped discovery: taking the shape the decision flowchart handed you (multi-writer, permissioned, tamper-evidence-focused, for example) and turning it into a specific technical and governance design: who operates validating nodes, who can write which fields, what happens when two parties disagree about a recorded value, and what the specific, measurable success criteria for a pilot will be. This stage produces a document, not code.

Stage two is the pilot program itself, deliberately narrow in scope: a small number of real participants, a defined time window, and success metrics fixed in advance, not adjusted after the fact to match whatever happened. This is also where you apply a technology readiness check: is the specific platform and vendor combination you're proposing mature enough for this use, or are you effectively becoming their first production reference customer while your executives think they're buying an established product? A pilot with a genuine sunset clause, meaning it is explicitly allowed to end in failure and be shut down, is the only kind of pilot that produces honest information; a pilot everyone has already decided must succeed just delays the failure and makes it more expensive.

Stage three is limited production: rolling out to a wider but still bounded set of participants, with monitoring in place to catch the problems that only show up at slightly larger scale, uneven data quality across writers, a participant who stops writing data reliably, disputes about a recorded value that the pilot never triggered. This stage is where governance gets tested for real, because pilot participants are usually hand-picked enthusiasts, and limited production brings in the first genuinely reluctant or skeptical participants whose behavior tells you whether the incentive design actually works.

Stage four is full rollout, which should look almost boring compared to the earlier stages: by this point the technology, the governance model, and the participant incentives have all already been validated at smaller scale, so full rollout is mostly an operations and change management exercise, not a technical gamble.

Return to Meridian Foods. Their decision flowchart output was a permissioned, multi-writer network among four known parties, optimized for tamper-evident temperature logging. Stage one discovery work settles concrete questions the flowchart never asked: will validating nodes run one per organization, giving each party equal weight, or weighted by shipment volume? What happens if the carrier's node goes offline during a shipment, does data queue until it reconnects or does another party's node need write access as a fallback? They decide on one validator per organization with a simple majority confirmation rule, and set the pilot's success criteria in advance: a high threshold of scheduled temperature readings captured without manual reentry over a defined pilot period, and zero disputes about a recorded value that can't be resolved using the system's own audit trail.

Stage two runs the pilot on a single lettuce supply route for one growing season, one grower, the carrier, and one retailer, deliberately excluding the other two retailers so the group can fail small if something goes wrong. Midway through, they discover the carrier's handheld scanners drop connectivity in certain rural stretches, producing gaps the system can't fill retroactively without looking exactly like the tampering it was built to prevent. That's a real finding a pilot is supposed to surface, and it sends the group back to stage one to add offline queuing with cryptographic timestamping at the point of capture, rather than at the point of network upload, before stage three even starts. Only after that fix is validated does Meridian move to limited production with all four original parties, and only after a full season of clean data at that scale does full rollout, bringing in additional retailers, become a change management project rather than a technology gamble.

The lesson underneath the specific stages is the same one that runs through this whole course: expensive commitments should follow evidence, not precede it. A roadmap that starts with a signed five-year vendor contract and only pilots afterward has the sequence backward.
